Penelope isn't one of those female leads that cries about everything and lets the world step on her once before deciding to finally throw a punch. It is one of those stories where the female lead is from a different world and is migrated into the new magical world the plot takes place in. However, what I think sets it apart from the rest is the constant reminder of the world's fakeness. From her past, the main lead female is actually introduced to all of the characters of the new world through an otome game she played during her spare hours. The game has 2 modes normal and hard (Penelope jokes that the normal mode is actually easy considering all the endings to each of the routes were easy as pie. After countless deaths in the game, she falls asleep to awake in the game as Penelope herself. However, unlike the game with retries, this time she can not retry and death was permanent.

I highly recommend this read (though some of the fan-translated chapters make you want to rip out your hair, it is still better than nothing at all). There are some scenes I do which I could have redone for clarity purposes but otherwise fantastic books. The side stories give me reasons to hate the characters I've learned to love so I'll have to drop it for the time being until I can handle getting though them. The Main story was conclusive but I do understand that unlocking all the routes' endings is the end goal. Overall best book of the year. Penelope has a place in my heart.

Title: Mate (Bride, #2)
Author: Ali Hazelwood
My Review:
I read Bride (Twice) and loved it both times. It's cliché with its many common tropes, sweet characters, and the spicy but tender romance. I ADORED IT.

This book... was very different in its approach. I, off the bat, completely hated both Serena and Koen. Koen because he was a special fucker.. an exceptional asshole, but he was truthful (ish) and dependable at the very least. Serena was a straight-up LIAR for the majority of the book. I could not understand for the life of me how Misery could jump into a marriage with the original intention of finding and reuniting with her adoptive sister and bestie Serena, but Serena, slowly crumpling with little to no time, refused to even share the rest of her time with Misery at the very least?? The selfishness was absolutely insane. I got why she felt as she did, but gods... I was finding it unbearable for the longest.

I was genuinely praying for someone to fold first cause the secondhand embarrassment I was experiencing through Serena was unfounded. Koen folded around the 50% mark, making the rest of the novel much more entertaining and a breath of hope for the story and characters. Koen and Serena's relationship was and is very rough and intense. It was vastly different from Lowe and Misery's relationship, which was much more titillating and romantic.

(I'm down bad for MiseryxLowe, so I loved every one of Misery's inclusion and involvement throughout the book. It was very grounding to see Misery and Serena's relationship bonding too.)

Truthfully, I gave Bride 4 stars originally, but even after the second read, it was entertaining and thoroughly scratched that nostalgic 2010s Wattpad-era itch. Therefore, I'd revised my rating to 5 stars. Now, regarding this book, it concluded well, and the story and lore were phenomenal. I loved how it was time-lined and switching back and forth till it caught up to the present. I loved the ongoing jokes, banter, and teasing. I just was not expecting so much more dark, intense lusting and roughness, it was almost borderline toxicity rather than mutual love.

Though it worked out, and honestly, it was a good ending. Since it did make me happy, especially the little nuances and moments that carried over from the first book, I did like the book overall. 4/5 stars for now, but that is subject to change as I see fit.

Title: Hot for Slayer
Author: Ali Hazelwood
My Review:
In honor of Valentine's Month(?) I decided to read this silly little book series Scared Sexy just for giggles so here's book one!

Clocking in at under 100 pages, this book had no business having as much depth and charm as it did. I’m a known sucker (pun fully intended) for enemies-to-lovers, and this delivered exactly what I crave. Tell me you wouldn’t fall a little bit for a man who’s had a massive crush on you for centuries—so intense that he hunts you down through time, stabs you every chance he gets just to see you, and would gladly kill anyone who gets in the way. Completely unhinged. Completely effective. I was in a chokehold.

Dirty jokes aside, I knew going in that this wouldn’t be a serious read, but it was genuinely fun. The story made it easy to imagine the centuries of pining and tangled obsession between these two long before the book ever begins. Ethyl’s backstory was surprisingly tragic and clearly explained her need to belong—to have people she could call her own. Lazlo’s backstory, particularly how his crush on Ethyl developed, was oddly adorable despite the violence baked into their dynamic. Against my better judgment, I fully condoned their murderous enemies-to-lovers arc.

The ending/climax reminded me of [b:Bride|181344829|Bride (Bride, #1)|Ali Hazelwood|https://i.gr-assets.com/images/S/compressed.photo.goodreads.com/books/1730451646l/181344829._SY75_.jpg|185069024] by Ali Hazelwood, and honestly? It worked. It felt natural (even if it's a paranormal story), satisfying, and perfectly tied up loose ends neatly. For something short, silly, and unapologetically chaotic, Hot for Slayer was an absolute delight.

Title: Spicy Little Curses
Author: J.T. Geissinger
My Review:
I’m genuinely conflicted about how to rate this one because it was better than [b:Falling|240583638|Falling|Christina Lauren|https://i.gr-assets.com/images/S/compressed.photo.goodreads.com/books/1769514015l/240583638._SX50_.jpg|258647220], but not more than [b:Hot for Slayer|240581511|Hot for Slayer|Ali Hazelwood|https://i.gr-assets.com/images/S/compressed.photo.goodreads.com/books/1756061884l/240581511._SY75_.jpg|258642212]. Maybe I'll have to go back and make adjustments to my ratings later as I see fit.

On one hand, I liked the story itself. The lore behind the curse was intriguing, and the eventual resolution felt thoughtful and emotionally grounded. I loved the world-building too, as it truly felt like the world of voodoo and dark magic, similar to The Princess and the Frog movie.

Dax fits squarely into the brooding, moody male archetype (which is to say he is quite basic despite his magically inked body)—burdened with a curse that causes any woman who falls in love with him to die. It’s dramatic, tragic, and very Halloween-coded. That part is fine.

Petra, however, was more complicated. I didn’t love the term of endearment “Notebook” (a nod to her being a journalist). It never quite landed as charming and instead felt awkward. I also struggled with her pushy nature at times; it wasn't charming in the slightest, seeing her cross his boundaries like it's nothing. That said, their banter was genuinely enjoyable—sharp, quick, and often the highlight of their dynamic. When they were simply talking, the chemistry felt fun.

My larger issue is structural.

This series consists of short Halloween-themed standalones written by different authors, each set in entirely separate worlds. They are not meant to overlap or build a shared universe. So it was frustrating that this story dropped hints of something much bigger—threads that felt like the start of a broader mythology—without resolving them. It ends with unanswered cliffhangers that suggest an expanding universe… but this is the universe. There’s nowhere else for those threads to go (unless I'm missing the memo that this story has a follow-up somewhere floating in the ether).

When I finished it, I thought it was fine—solid, entertaining, and resolved enough. But sitting with it a day later, the open-ended implications don’t feel satisfying. They feel incomplete.

I enjoyed the curse lore. I liked the central premise. I appreciated the banter. But the tonal and structural choices—especially for what’s supposed to be a contained standalone—leave me uncertain.

So for now, it sits somewhere in the middle. Not a miss, but not okay.

Title: Falling
Author: Christina Lauren
My Review:
That ending was criminal.

It honestly took until the pub conversations for me to feel genuinely invested in their (Brigan, our fallen angel, and Catalina) relationship. Up until then, the physical attraction was obvious, and the chemistry was there, but it wasn’t enough to fully pull me in. It was those quieter moments—being honest over drinks, trading witty banter, actually talking—that made them feel real. That’s when I started rooting for them.

Which is exactly why the abrupt ending was so frustrating.

The story cuts off just shy of any meaningful resolution. For something that hinges on a curse, there’s surprisingly little clarity about how it could be broken—or if it even was. Are we supposed to assume Brigan’s curse was somehow undone? Was she meant to become immortal to stay with him? None of it is clearly addressed, which makes the conclusion feel incomplete rather than open-ended.

I wouldn’t say I hated the book, but I disliked it. The stakes were relatively low (considering this is just a silly Romance series set in Halloween that I'm reading in the wrong season, but I digress), and there were genuinely enjoyable moments. But coming off [b:Hot for Slayer|240581511|Hot for Slayer|Ali Hazelwood|https://i.gr-assets.com/images/S/compressed.photo.goodreads.com/books/1756061884l/240581511._SY75_.jpg|258642212], which had surprising depth, satisfying character arcs, and a conclusive ending, my expectations were clearly set high for the series overall. In comparison, this one felt underdeveloped—particularly in its final act.

The potential was there. The emotional groundwork was there. The execution at the end just didn’t quite follow through for me.

For now, I’ll mentally fantasize and give the characters the ending they deserve.

Title: Emily Wilde’s Map of the Otherlands (Emily Wilde, #2)
Author: Heather Fawcett
My Review:
Emily Wilde’s Map of the Otherlands was just as fantastical as the first book, though notably less cozy in atmosphere. The moments of humor and calm between Emily and Wendell were present, but far more sparingly. The overall story had a sharper sense of tension and urgency which makes sense because poor Wendell got poisoned on his birthday of all days (no this isnt a spoiler it happens within the first two chapters).

Emily continues to be the novel’s greatest strength. Her intelligence and resourcefulness are repeatedly emphasized, especially in contrast to Rose, whose role as both antagonist and uneasy ally highlights how consistently capable Emily is. I did wish Ariadne had been more involved, but her limited role ultimately made sense—she remains too young to be pivotal until her fresh perspective becomes necessary to move the plot forward.

The underlying lore surrounding the missing scholars, De Grey and Eichorn, was intriguing, but it ultimately became my greatest frustration with the book. By the end, they felt more like the fae who tormented them than the scholars they once were. I had hoped they would represent a breakthrough—answers, clarity, or even active resistance—but instead we relied solely on Emily to figure it out by herself. She is brilliant, but I find it a tiny bit of stretch for her to solve a decades-old mystery in a couple of weeks. While this reinforced Emily’s strength as a protagonist, it made their long-anticipated presence feel underwhelming.

Speaking of underwhelming, I had not expected Wendell’s stepmother to be that careless especially after giving her grand speech of mortals being the dangerous ones despite Faeries having such power, numbers and strength. That whole interaction was well meaning to show how prepared Emily was, but still.. Maybe as a reader I had expected a longer fight between two mortals involved in Faerie court systems.

That said, the novel does an excellent job of setting the stage for what’s to come. With war looming and the next book poised to explore a fight for the throne, I’m eager to see how the suspicious “saviors” from the Summer Court will help—or harm—our protagonists when the stakes are no longer purely academic, but political and deadly.

While less cozy than its predecessor, Map of the Otherlands expands the world, sharpens its conflicts, and leaves the series on a compelling precipice that makes the next installment impossible not to anticipate.

Title: Overruled
Author: Lana Ferguson
My Review:
It legitimately took me 3 weeks to get into just 20% of this book. It finally started picking up for me after seeing just how dysfunctional Ezra's family is and how he copes to keep me from losing it, coping with Dani's indecisions/defensiveness. I made several comments throughout the first and mid-part of the book about the characters honestly seeking therapy. Dani's inability to work through and face her abandonment issues and relationship trauma was frustrating to the point I could not enjoy the book for the longest part.

I honestly read the rest of the 80% in one day (crazy enough, the ball kept rolling once it started). I think I was being harsh with Dani's defensiveness and avoiding the issues she had head-on. Ezra's issues, I can see how hard he was cornered, especially with how unsupported he is professionally and personally.

The good about the book outweighed the rough start.

I'm glad the issues were worked through slowly but surely throughout the book with a satisfying ending. I liked the interactions between the two leads and their biting banter. I, would have loved a more charming first impression of Dani, but she got better as she started to process and unpack her traumas. When things got intense between the two of them, it got INTENSE. On a side note, I loved Nate and Vera's quips and supportive roles. I'll miss them when I think back on this book in the future. The case being solved and disputed was also very much satisfying to see close and open up new opportunities. The Casaragi case was a bit bland, but I adored Mrs.Casaragi's strength and resolve to bring that Lorenzo scumbag to his knees. It was genuinely satisfying to see how things unfolded and the plot thickened.

Title: Not Quite Dead Yet
Author: Holly  Jackson
My Review:
I knew how this would end. We were warned in the synopsis and again in the opening chapters. And still, when it finally happened, it shocked me and left me heartbroken.

Watching Jet fall apart—even as she kept reminding herself and us that she was dying—was devastating. The moment that hurt the most was her final realization about Billy: initially suspecting him, knowing deep down he wasn’t the one, and choosing peace over answers. He wanted to tell her something just so she could have closure, but Jet was already complete by then. That unrequited love between them made me bitter in the way only a hopeless romantic can be. She knew it wasn’t in their stars and wanted him to find new ones—and that acceptance hurt more than denial ever could.

Billy ended up being the emotional backbone of the story, and I regret my early impressions of him (a nerdy, quiet guy just trying to shoot his shot). I adored his own silent grieving and bonding with Jet till the end. Jet’s dark, copium humor pulled me in immediately, and I found myself relating to her more than I expected—the belief that there’s always more time, the way commitments get postponed, the restless search for something to do. I felt miserably hopeless alongside her, and it made her final days—so productive, so honest—feel both refreshing and unfair.

Her letters absolutely destroyed me. I truly cried the most when I read her handwritten letters for her family and loved ones. It tied up her story neatly, though not all answers would be given by the end of the book.

The ending is one I both love and hate. I hated the funeral. I hated that there was a funeral at all. I hated the small, irrational part of me that hoped for a miracle. But the more I sat with it, the more it felt inevitable—something Jet herself seemed to understand. Her heartbreak wasn’t just for herself, but for Billy and the ending of a story they never truly got to live.

I didn’t love how everything "resolved" at first, especially the final act of violence, but with time I appreciated the sense of consequence. I needed to let my mind stew on the consequences and climax at the end of the story, it truly went to shit there Billy... No one escapes untouched. Everyone moves toward the ending they’ve earned, whether on the page or implied beyond it. That quiet closure is what ultimately made it work for me. (spoilers here:

Title: My Friends
Author: Fredrik Backman
My Review:
I fell in love with the way this book is written—the way the words flow so naturally they feel less like prose and more like a quiet conversation between me and the page. There’s an intimacy to the narration that makes you forget you’re reading at all; instead, you’re listening, remembering, feeling alongside it.

I adored how the story is slowly chipped away and revealed, how moments echo across chapters, resurfacing later with deeper meaning. It’s the kind of storytelling that trusts the reader—to notice, to remember, to feel. I don’t even think I’m competent enough to fully articulate how emotional this book made me, or how deeply enamored I became with those teenagers on the pier, with Louisa and Ted, as their lives stretched across time and distance.

Reading [b:My Friends|217163697|My Friends|Fredrik Backman|https://i.gr-assets.com/images/S/compressed.photo.goodreads.com/books/1734625930l/217163697._SY75_.jpg|223642719] felt like being wrapped in a hug from my childhood. I craved this book like a swim on a hot summer day, a cold soda after a run, and a bedtime story under cozy, soft sheets. How the hell did I go my entire life without reading this masterpiece?

The way these people loved and lived was both awe-inspiring and devastatingly beautiful. I cried constantly while reading—grieving and cherishing the small, precious memories that stayed with Ted throughout his life: the bird they saved, the shopping cart rides, the art competition used as a distraction, and swimming in the sea. I felt Joar’s pain so sharply—the quiet devastation of being beaten down by a bitter, cripple-minded old man who projected his own insecurity and unhappiness onto a child. I ached over the way Ali chose to trust and believe in the boys after everything that had been done to her. I mourned alongside Ted and C. Jat, whose grief wasn’t physical but mental—a loss that consumed them through silence, memory, and distance. The emotional blocks and barriers these teens endured felt heartbreakingly real. I was right beside Lousia as we experienced everything in those moments that had already happened in our present together.

I completely broke down at the end, realizing I wouldn’t get to see them all grow old together, still smiling. I was right beside Lousia the entire time.

What I’m struggling to explain—what feels almost impossible to put into words—is that my heart hadn’t experienced this kind of feeling from a book before. The closest I can come is this: there is a life before My Friends, and now there is a life after it. And I don’t know how to endure the after without carrying this story with me.

I simply couldn’t put it down, and hands down, it will probably be my favorite book of the year.

Title: Apprentice to the Villain (Assistant to the Villain, #2)
Author: Hannah Nicole Maehrer
My Review:
I picked up Apprentice to the Villain immediately after finishing [b:Assistant to the Villain|123257687|Assistant to the Villain (Assistant to the Villain, #1)|Hannah Nicole Maehrer|https://i.gr-assets.com/images/S/compressed.photo.goodreads.com/books/1702057336l/123257687._SY75_.jpg|144626864], and I knew exactly what I was getting into. The book definitely maintained the tone and charm of the first installment, and I was happy to spend more time with the side characters as their secrets slowly came to light. I like the small friendship between Blade and Trystan forming while Becky and Evie were starting to patch up their differences, too. That said, I couldn’t shake the feeling that there was a lot of missed potential. While romance was in the air, disaster was too, starting with too many things happening to the characters rather than happening because of them. Consequences felt light, and progression often came too easily, even when obstacles were introduced.

That issue became clearer with the book’s increasing reliance on destiny. Evie getting the job, surviving the death-fruit—both are retroactively framed as destiny’s interference rather than earned outcomes. By the epilogue, destiny is positioned as the driving force behind not just past events, but future ones as well. Gideon’s belief that the Story of Rennedawn may point to Evie as the unmasked Villain reframes the prophecy entirely, while the Creature of Destiny’s warning—that Trystan would be her undoing and she his making—pushes Trystan into the conclusion that separation is the only way to protect her but that may not mean anything if she's the prophesized villain. The result is a narrative where inevitability starts to overshadow agency, and character decisions feel less like choices and more like reactions to prophecy.

The pining between Trystan and Evie initially worked for me, but the prolonged "will-they-won't-they" separation started to wear thin. At a certain point, the “unrequited love” angle felt unbelievable—everyone around them could see they were clearly in love except for the two of them. It crossed from yearning into outright delusion. Evie, whom I previously admired for her communication, seemed to lose that strength entirely in this book, which was frustrating. Additionally, I also always saw Evie in a bloodthirsty type light, so her sudden bloodlust wasn't shocking to me as it seems to be to the others. I'm just holding out on her messing with Trystan in the next book to the point he has to admit to her he's in love.

Okay, but some of the iconic moments between Evie and Trystan that happened in this book still have me in a complete chokehold well after the ending. I can’t even believe I’m saying this, but Trystan is a massive green flag when it comes to consent. His vigilance around it genuinely made me feral in the best and worst way. The fact that he refused to kiss or take advantage of Evie when she was drunk—even when it felt like they might be facing their last moments—had me fuming and giggling through actual tears. It was infuriating. It was tender. It was everything. This sentiment is truly what carried me through the book.

Despite the irritation, the angst still hit hard. Some moments were truly heart-wrenching, even if a few pushed my patience to its limits. And honestly? I enjoyed the suffering enough that I’ll absolutely be picking up the next book. Flaws and all, I’m still invested.

Title: Assistant to the Villain (Assistant to the Villain, #1)
Author: Hannah Nicole Maehrer
My Review:
I truly did not expect Assistant to the Villain to blow me away the way it did. The comedy is very tongue-in-cheek, and I genuinely had a good time with it. Most of the jokes were fun, and even when they didn’t fully land, they still earned a smile or scoff through sheer cringe, corniness, or deliberate stupidity.

That said, the secondhand embarrassment at the beginning was rough. I side-eyed nearly every decision Evie Sage made. This girl was THIRSTING for The Villain when she and we readers practically knew nothing about him, including his name. The starting humor is kind of dirty-minded humor, but honestly, it’s still okay (barely) because it's all taken as lighthearted nonsense (because our gal Evie Sage just loves rambling). But slowly, very slowly, her infectious, cheery nature and earnestness won me over. I was concerned at my first impressions of her when she kinda shrugged off harassment, abuse, and sexism for the longest time. I’m looking back at the comments and highlights of the book, and I definitely started liking Evie around chapter 20. By the end, I could genuinely see myself being her friend if I lived in this world, which is wild now that I see all the harsh comments and judgment I was giving her in the first 20 chapters.

The Villain himself was interesting—but he wasn’t actually a villain. He was dark and broody with banter and sarcasm to boot, but it just wasn’t villainous enough. I really wish his backstory had been revealed much earlier, because learning it roughly five percent from the end made it difficult to fully understand his role in the story, the plot, and his relationships with other characters. (I watched a book review with The Book Leo and she’s so real for saying that he’s literally a badass like Uncle Iroh escaping the way he did). I didn’t think too much into how he monologued his past majority of the time, but it's kind of a cop out in a way to chop up his character like that to keep character moments short (the book was 60-some chapters, it's okay to have more pages describing characters more with more to them). His reactions and inner thoughts in response to Evie’s chaos were endlessly entertaining, but despite the title, he never actively commits any crimes within the book. Everything is framed as an action fantasy unfolding largely within an office setting—and I’ll admit, office romances are a soft spot for me, even though I don’t indulge in them often.

What truly sold me, however, was the restraint in Evie and the Villain’s relationship. The chaste, slow-burn affection they share—right up until the final moments—made every interaction feel intentional and meaningful. And the ending? I was outraged to the point of tears. I will be reading book two. That is a promise I’m holding myself to.

This book is very plot-driven, and the characters genuinely cannot catch a break—something is always happening, which I’m not mad about. It keeps my mind busy trying to juggle all the things going on as an overarching story takes place in the forefront. The mystery surrounding the mole in the office was a major highlight for me. I was pointing fingers just as wildly as Evie, if not more. The reveal had me ready to throw hands on her behalf.

I also appreciated how the book handled trauma. It’s approached with care and respect, without forcing emotional confessions just for dramatic payoff. Evie holds back until she’s ready, and when she finally opens up, it doesn’t feel rushed or pressured. The Villain—despite the title—is calm, attentive, and genuinely listens before reacting. He isn’t a cookie-cutter villain, but I wouldn’t call him deeply written either; much of his internal conflict comes from suppressing his affection for Evie and prioritizing revenge. Book two better not give me the “obvious ending”—I want the true villain exposed and our “Villain” to earn his redemption.

And I have to mention the two scenes that had me absolutely giggling. The goofy cover-up story Evie made to get everyone to safety had me dying. I was already smiling and laughing at her acting as the dramatic wife to the Villain, as he lay unconscious. But then he was starting to wake up and she's thinking “Frick he's gonna wake up and murder everyone, I need to shut him up now-” and kisses him without hesitation. THIS MAN LEGIT THOUGHT IT WAS A DREAM and CONTINUED TO MAKE OUT PUBLICLY INFRONT OF STANGERS, HIS FAMILY, AND FRIENDS. The way I started cackling and tearing up from how publicly this man was enamored by Evie, and she was just like “oh thank gods you heard the made-up story I gave the knights to let us go.” He's shocked, going a 100 miles a minute, letting his soul catch up to how he just made out with Evie and called her his love in public with everyone to see. It was, in fact, not a dream at all.

The second was the hug they shared after the mole was revealed, which had my heart racing. It was deeply intimate without being smutty—just pure yearning. And I am an absolute sucker for yearning.

I really liked this book, but I can see how it might not be for everyone, especially because you’d have to tough it out for 25% of the book and be blind to its shortcomings in character depth.

Title: Witch Hat Atelier, Vol. 1
Author: Kamome Shirahama
My Review:
I’ll be honest I really picked it up initially because of how beautiful the cover looked. The art as well was STUNNING. The story and magic system is what sold it for me though completely. In a world where everyone could potentially use magic it because clear that when anyone could do anything they would do anything. This led to essentially an all out war and it ended with powerful wizards/witches coming together to create the idea that you needed to be born with an affinity to magic to use it.. they erased everyone’s memories and created a system that certain magic that hurt people would never be practiced.

This is where our lead comes in to the story. Coco adores magic and buys a book and pen to learn it.. She wishes desperately to have the ability to use it but being told she wasn’t born with the power she copes with the shortcoming with fantasies. She stays with her mom and tailors clothes to perfection until one day she witnesses how magic is actually performed..

She pulls out the pen/wand and begins tracing the spells in the book and realizes she in fact can use magic. The whole situation sours immediately when a spell goes wrong and her mother is caught in the aftermath.. the book destroyed and her mother lost to magic she is forced to become a witch and recover the book and save her mother.


The magical society is incredibly nuanced and deeply flawed in how it shelters itself but it’s reasonable to see why magic is gated and its knowledge not shared.. Coco faced prejudices and ostracized for her sudden apprenticeship due to her consequences of using forbidden magic unknowingly.. it makes for a really interesting story and I can’t wait to see how she flourishes using the skills her mother taught her and her potential to change the magical and non-magical society forever. (chapter 4 was my absolute favorite)

Title: Wolves and Daggers (The Red Cape Society, #1)
Author: Melanie Karsak
My Review:
I was initially interested at this new twist retelling of Little Red Riding Hood. A lupine disease that turns humans into werewolves, but their weakness being silver still. Little Red Riding Hood herself is part of a secret special force under the Queen protecting people against threats. That’s unfortunately where my liking comes to end.

Louvel is stagnant as a character with literally no growth in character from start to finish. She complains constantly about not having a man to handle her needs, but proceeds to make no changes or progress towards alleviating her issues. She’s simply admiring her fellow/enemy werewolves and lusting for them while also keeping herself in check. It’s quite annoying to see her bring up wanting a man every other chapter and her friends in the force and her grand mere even mention eligible bachelors, but she declines due to work. At the end of the book, she basically promises to continue serving on the frontlines as soon as she recovers (pushing her directly and further into a work heavy lifestyle). She’s never getting a man nor is she ever making an effort to change it, but will 100% complain about it.

Agent Quinn made the most sense in the book to be honest. He worked hard and while doing that tried balancing his home life. He gets into a grave situation so much so that he outright makes a decision that I completely understand. His intentions, motivations and actions all made a lot of sense and were completely reasonable. I enjoyed his character the most and it’s kinda tragic knowing he was basically present for maybe 20% of the book at best?

I didn’t like how the author addressed and treated female werewolves in the prostitution business. I have some heavy highlights and comments on the chapter where Agent Louvel goes to the brothel and depicts all the workers as whores and tarts.. First of all that was highly uncalled for, she could have just easily explained her uncomfortable feelings about being there considering she has not had a man in a hot minute as she loves to complain about and how she would have wished they had some other kind of service rather than selling themselves. She then was assaulted by a customer who thought she was a new werewolf sex worker and she defended herself rightfully. However, rather than a fellow female defending against the customer’s poor excuse for consent the female werewolves basically kick her out the door bc of the silver dagger in her hands. Like girl be for real right now. I get the werewolves on edge about the weapon, but at least talk it out..? In my opinion they should have told the customer off for his behavior and told her she is not welcome simply because of her weapon and inability to leave the weapons off their property. The way they all essentially kind of at the very least treat each other with bare minimum respect.


I don’t know.. I just didn’t like how the story pacing was handled nor the nuances of social and political dynamics between the different characters. I won’t be continuing the series anytime soon.

Title: Red Queen (Red Queen, #1)
Author: Victoria Aveyard
My Review:
For a politically dense fantasy novel, The Red Queen delivers a surprisingly smooth reading experience. The environment itself is one of the book’s strongest elements—the brutality between Silvers and Reds, the atmosphere of chaos, and the tension of a nation at war all feel vividly constructed. The way the Silvers treat the Reds as nothing more than expendable bodies for their war efforts is infuriating in the best way; the cruelty is portrayed so sharply that I often found myself angry on behalf of the Reds. The scale of the oppression, the segregation, and the systemic conditioning is shocking, yet the clever ways the Reds take advantage of the Silvers’ fear of the unknown add an undercurrent of resistance that I appreciated.

Despite how strong the world is, I absolutely despised Mare. She may have been cornered into her situation, but her behavior should have led her to be far more guarded—especially around Silvers who have victimized her entire life. Instead, she reveals everything far too easily. She's extremely naive despite the education she's finally receiving. To make matters worse, she isn’t the only one whose choices raised questions; the Red Guard accepting the prince’s target selections without deeper investigation, research, or surveillance made their operations feel reckless. It’s one of the few areas where the character decisions weakened the logic of the rebellion. I didn't understand Kilorn at all either. Why would he go out of his way to seek danger when he's never been the type to make those decisions before? So many people's decisions and actions did not sit well with me.

The twist, however, was executed extremely well. It crept up slowly, and once the full scope of the scheme came into view, the depth and reach of the betrayal hit hard.

Cal, on the other hand, left me with mixed emotions. As much as he operates with caution and thinks like a future king, he missed nearly every sign of the schemes unfolding around the throne. He genuinely wants to make a nation worth unifying and building stronger for everyone, but he couldn't protect his people. He was played the entire time, and I genuinely felt the worst for him—there’s a real sense of trauma in how thoroughly he was deceived. His sense of statesmanship completely failed him, and instead of spending so much time training, he should have been reading the political landscape, recognizing manipulation, and questioning his mother and brother rather than giving them the benefit of the doubt. What's done is done and now he needs to figure out how to take a stand for what he believes.

Despite these frustrations with the characters, the writing remains clean and accessible. The political depth, social hierarchy, and strategic tension give the story weight. I do wish the mutation behind Mare’s blood and her unique circumstances had been explained in greater detail, though that seems intentionally reserved for later in the series.

Overall, The Red Queen combines rebellion, romance, inequality, and political intrigue into a compelling narrative, made stronger by its world-building and sharper by its betrayals.

Title: Emily Wilde's Encyclopaedia of Faeries (Emily Wilde, #1)
Author: Heather Fawcett
My Review:
Emily Wilde’s Encyclopedia of Faeries begins as a meticulous researcher’s field journal but gradually unfolds into a charming blend of scholarship, adventure, and emotional growth. It took time to truly settle into Emily’s voice—she presents herself as cold, detached, and wholly committed to her work—but that distance feels intentional. Yes, I do see why some may say it is overly written, but that's honestly the point because she means to use her journal as a means to define and recall details of her day-to-day events in her book and research later. Watching her writing gradually soften when she accepts companionship and recognizes that she no longer carries the weight of her life alone gave her arc a satisfying emotional payoff.

The story’s strength lies in how every plot element earns its place. Early observations, words of power, and seemingly simple interactions later thread directly into the major conflicts. Emily’s dog Shadow, Poe’s involvement in the unraveling mysteries, and the villagers’ resilience all play deliberate roles. Every detail matters, and the cumulative effect is rewarding.

Wendell Bambleby’s arrival is where the book truly comes alive. His banter, wit, and chaotic warmth contrast sharply with Emily’s precision, creating a dynamic that energizes every scene they share. The turning point in their relationship unfolds when he willingly follows her into danger to rescue the two girls and later helps return a changeling—moments that reveal his devotion beneath the theatrics. His choice to share more of his fae identity with her adds depth, sincerity, and a surprising vulnerability. Over time, he shifts from mildly tolerable to genuinely endearing, his presence adding charm without overshadowing Emily’s journey. Their connection is written with restraint yet undeniable chemistry, and Emily’s refusal to be swayed by surface-level charm only makes their growing bond more compelling.

The village setting adds both charm and tension: an isolated community haunted by fae threats, particularly in winter. Emily’s involvement shifts from professional curiosity to genuine care, and her bond with the villagers becomes one of the most touching aspects of the story. The women, in particular, stand strong—unyielding, practical, and shaped by hardship. There are no weak links here.

The writing style blends academic journaling with narrative progression in a way that feels fresh and accessible. The gaps and unreliable moments in Emily’s entries give the story texture without sacrificing coherence. The faerie lore itself is beautifully woven, filled with danger, enchantment, and folkloric logic that stays clear without over-explaining. The daring escape from the faerie king and the larger consequences for the region deliver a well-executed finale.

I do have to say that the ending feels intentionally unfinished. Emily’s response to Wendell, the looming ICODEF conference results, and the uncertain future of Wendell’s lost place at home all point toward larger stakes that remain unresolved. Those threads create anticipation rather than frustration, leaving plenty of room for their evolving partnership—personal, magical, and possibly political.

In all, this was an immersive and rewarding read—slow to start, but rich, clever, and full of character. I’ll gladly continue the series, especially to see where Emily and Wendell’s complicated bond leads next.

Title: The Pumpkin Spice Café (Dream Harbor, #1)
Author: Laurie Gilmore
My Review:
The Pumpkin Spice Café was an easy, cozy fall read with some heat to it. I listened to the audiobook while reading the paperback, and the combination added a warm, atmospheric touch that suited the story’s autumn vibe perfectly.

This is a straightforward small-town romance: a new woman in town taking over a café, a very attractive farmer next door, and a slow shift from strangers to something more. I didn’t approach this book expecting depth or emotional weight—just something seasonal and fun—and it delivered exactly that.

Both main characters were surprisingly well-developed for a light read. Their chemistry sparks fast, but the conflicts and misunderstandings that follow felt believable within the story’s pace. I never felt annoyed or disconnected from their choices, which made it easy to stay invested. The cozy town setting and fall atmosphere were charming as well.

There were a few cheesy moments and some scenes that leaned a little too spicy for my taste, but overall, it was an enjoyable, warm seasonal read that fit perfectly with the autumn mood.

I’m leaning towards a 3.5 stars on this one leaning towards a 4. It was fun and I might pick up the other books in the series if I feel like it. Otherwise this was a good standalone.

Title: Ruthless Vows (Letters of Enchantment, #2)
Author: Rebecca   Ross
My Review:
Ruthless Vows was everything I wanted in a sequel and ending. It picks up three weeks after Divine Rivals and drops you right back into the war that's brewing into something worse by the minute. It felt heavy in all the right ways — not everything was okay, but there was this sense of people trying to heal, both physically and emotionally, after everything Dacre’s tyranny destroyed.

The pacing was steady and deliberate. It picked up when it needed to, especially during the chaos of the western front or the underground battle scenes. Waiting for Roman to escape and find his way back to Iris felt unbearable at times — in a good way. Every delay, every near miss made the eventual resolution that much more rewarding.

Iris and Roman’s relationship starting over was so beautifully done. She remembers him, but he has to slowly rediscover what they had. Watching him fall for her again completely melted me. Their love feels timeless — that slow, old-fashioned yearning that so many stories skip over now. It’s patient, earned, and incredibly romantic.

I liked Tobias a lot, especially his quiet affection for Attie. I just wish we’d seen more of Forest and Sarah Prindle. There weren’t many light moments, but it makes sense — they’re still in the heart of war and all its aftermath. I wanted more happiness for them, but grief and recovery were part of the story’s truth.

Rebecca Ross’s writing was as emotional and lyrical as ever, but with more weight this time. Every choice mattered — saving someone, betraying someone, staying or leaving. I personally didn't hate Dacre much until his manipulation was clear and irrefutable. I held him in contempt for the rest of the novel. Her tone definitely shifted darker compared to Divine Rivals, showing how cruel Dacre really was and how desperately Enva fought to break free from him and free others from his grasp.

It’s not a perfect world by the end, but it’s a fitting one. The typewriters are gone, the scars remain, and yet there’s still something whole about the way it all closes. It’s bittersweet — but it feels right, extremely heartbreakingly sad, but right.

Honestly, both books stand side by side for me. Divine Rivals gave us the spark; Ruthless Vows gave us the weight of everything that spark had to survive. Easily one of my favorite duologies of the year.

Title: The Banned Books Club
Author: Brenda Novak
My Review:
The Banned Books Club by Brenda Novak explores family, trauma, and resilience in a small town where silence often speaks louder than truth.

I’ll admit, it took me a while to get into this book. I used the audiobook to help push through the start since I wasn’t relating to Gia or her sister Margot at first. It was frustrating to see Gia abandon her family after the events with Mr. Hart, but as the story unfolded, I understood her decision better. No one had stood up for her, and the weight of that isolation made her flight believable. The same goes for Margot, trapped in a marriage with a manipulative, verbally abusive husband.

The pacing leaned heavily toward the emotional drama, while the romance subplot felt rushed and somewhat unearned. I found it surprising — even uncomfortable — that Gia fell in love with her former abuser’s son. The scenes that hit hardest for me were the trial transcript and the harassment sequences. The audacity of Mr. Hart continuing to lie after seventeen years, and the incompetence of the local cops (who were conveniently friends with Sheldon), genuinely infuriated me.

Gia herself grew on me slowly. Her impulsiveness annoyed me early on, but I respected how she faced her trauma head-on by standing up to Sheldon and protecting her sister from repeating the same mistakes. That full-circle moment brought closure and emotional payoff.

Thematically, the book handled trauma and small-town stigma realistically. It never felt melodramatic — just deeply frustrating in ways that mirror real life. The “banned books” club, however, was more symbolic than central. It represented Gia’s defiance and voice against oppression, but it barely appeared in the story (maybe three percent at most). As a title, it felt misleading.

In the end, I liked that all the loose ends tied up neatly though in a very rushed way. Ida and Leo’s scenes offered warmth and hope amid the heavier subjects. The story’s takeaway was clear: family is forged through loyalty, not blood, and speaking out against injustice is difficult but necessary.

This book will likely appeal to readers interested in stories about confronting trauma, family loyalty, and small-town hypocrisy. It’s light reading, but it does leave you with a sense of justice and emotional closure.

Title: Forget Me Not
Author: Stacy Willingham
My Review:
Stacy Willingham’s Forget Me Not is a slow-burning mystery-thriller that unravels generational trauma, buried secrets, and the long-reaching consequences of violence and corruption. At the heart of the story is Claire Campbell, an investigative journalist who returns to her hometown in South Carolina after 22 years, still haunted by the disappearance of her older sister, Natalie. Taking a summer job at Galloway Farm—the last place Natalie was seen—Claire uncovers a diary that points to a much darker legacy than she expected.

Overall, I really liked the plot. While the pacing was slow at times, it was also deliberate and rewarding. Each chapter gave me something new, and I found myself genuinely drawn in by how each revelation fit slowly and perfectly into place. The journal entries were especially well-placed; they gave depth and tension to the story without overwhelming Claire’s voice in the present.

Claire herself felt real, if sometimes frustrating. She was understandably sluggish in her investigation at first, weighed down by grief and emotional stagnation. But I couldn’t blame her—her life was shaped by an unresolved trauma, and Willingham did a great job of showing how that can twist memory and motivation. The whole small-town atmosphere added to the closed-door, locked-in feeling of the story. The supporting characters were varied and essential to the story, though I didn’t feel particularly connected to Ryan, whose role felt underdeveloped. I was far more invested in Claire’s journey to get closer to her sister’s truth.

One of the book’s strengths is its unflinching portrayal of difficult themes: trafficking, grooming, abuse, generational trauma, and the failures of systems meant to protect the vulnerable. Claire’s childlike obsession to be like her sister to understand her better becomes a complicated mix of guilt and misunderstanding following her 22 years. Characters like Marcia and Annie show how trauma never really leaves, even after escape. The corruption within the law enforcement system adds another layer of injustice, and I appreciated that the book never shied away from those hard realities.

And then there's Lily. From the moment she appeared in Marcia’s diary, I hated her—and that hatred only deepened. She embodied everything twisted and cruel about the world Claire was investigating, and my visceral reaction to her speaks volumes about Willingham’s ability to write compelling (and detestable) villains.

In the end, I was relieved to see justice served. It's a story that honors the weight of the past. It's like Natalie’s favorite flower, the forget-me-nots—delicate, persistent, and impossible to ignore, even after decades, the truth resurfaced. If you’re looking for a thriller that’s atmospheric, emotionally layered, and socially aware, this one is worth the read.

Title: One Dark Window (The Shepherd King, #1)
Author: Rachel Gillig
My Review:
One Dark Window by Rachel Gillig felt like stepping into a dark fairytale — cozy, mysterious, and filled with a lush, misty atmosphere that pulled me in from the first chapter. The story’s magical system and gothic world were beautifully woven together, almost like revisiting childhood stories but with higher stakes and a haunting undertone.

I genuinely enjoyed the dynamic between Elspeth and the Nightmare. He was equal parts witty, sarcastic, and strangely reliable — honestly, she should’ve listened to him more often. Elspeth’s hesitancy and lack of initiative sometimes grated on me, but considering how she was raised to hide and stay quiet, her behavior made sense. Their bond, though unconventional, became one of my favorite parts of the book — two beings relying on each other in ways that blurred the line between protector and partner.

Ravyn Yew irritated me at first, but somewhere along the way I warmed up to him. Their relationship was a slow burn that surprised me once things finally started moving. Elm and Jespyr added much-needed humor and heart, even if Jespyr sometimes felt underused. Ione, on the other hand, left me conflicted — her change after the card felt punishing and confusing in a way that lingered.

The Providence Cards were a fascinating piece of lore — each one carried a moral weight and consequence that tied beautifully into the story’s theme that magic always has a cost. That cost hits hard by the ending, which left me tense and a little heartbroken.

Overall, One Dark Window is a hauntingly beautiful tale of power, sacrifice, and self-acceptance. The writing style perfectly matched the gothic tone, and October turned out to be the perfect month to read it. I’d recommend it to anyone who loves YA fantasy, fairytales, and morally gray magic with emotional depth.

And yes — I’ll definitely be picking up Two Twisted Crowns.

Title: Payback's a Witch (The Witches of Thistle Grove #1)
Author: Lana Harper
My Review:
I honestly didn’t like the main character at all. Emmy couldn’t make a coherent decision until the very last chapter, and she built her entire self-esteem and confidence around a crappy high school ex. To make matters worse, that ex is basically the town’s community bike—yet she’s the one spiraling about her own self-worth?

Honestly, i hated Emmy for hurting all of her family and Linden by leaving so abruptly/selfishly. I can't see a scenario of me leaving my childhood home, family and town i love dearly just bc of a man(nah a damn boy) others praise highly from my hs days. hell no he isn't the center of my universe to be making decisions around him.

I also didn’t see much genuine chemistry between the two leads outside of physical attraction and lust for about 60% of the book. Communication, which is such a key relationship skill, was completely absent—no one was ever cutthroat honest with Emmy, which made the romance feel flat let alone the town’s inhabitants relationship with her. Apparently it’s a close knit small town, but there's really just 3 girls(Linden, Talia and Emmy) and 2 boys (Rowan and Gareth) centering the whole book. Others either just popped in once every 6 chapters before disappearing again for long stretched.

While the lore and magical contests for generational powers were fun, that aspect was overshadowed by Emmy’s self-centered and self-inflicted tragedies.

I don’t think I’ll continue with the series, but maybe I’ll give it another shot someday if I have nothing else to read or it’s conveniently available.

Title: 花と銀 1 [Hana to Gin 1]
Author: Hidebu Takahashi
My Review:
Vol. 1 (Chapters 1–10.5)
Genre: BL, Romantic Comedy, Crime Drama

Let me start by saying—Hana and Gin are charming. Their chemistry is immediate, magnetic, and just the right mix of sweet and chaotic. This BL romantic comedy takes the familiar trope of opposites attract and layers it with crime drama, undercover work, and a heavy dose of unresolved tension.

The series follows two former police officers: Hanai, who’s joined the yakuza, and Gin, now a private detective. I wasn’t expecting the BL elements to be this strong—not just in subtext, but in almost every character dynamic. It’s wild how every man seems to want Hanai, but honestly… he is fine as hell, so I get it to a degree.

What surprised me most was how well the series handles emotional depth. Hanai, secretly still working undercover, adds an unexpected twist. His internal conflict—being torn between duty and his growing feelings for Gin—gives the story real weight. He's meant to keep his emotions in check while keeping tabs on his own yakuza clan and the other clans' actions in the meantime.. However, it's looking like those feelings for his buddy Gin are not just flirtation; there’s something sincere simmering beneath the surface.

Chapter 9 really stuck with me. When Hanai says, "A man dying in love may not be such a bad thing," it hit different. He’s conflicted, sure, but it’s obvious he’s catching real feelings for the cute detective Gin. It's moments like that that give this series heart beyond its humor and hotness.

All in all, Volume 1 sets a solid foundation. It’s lusty, dramatic, and surprisingly thoughtful. I do hope there will be more light shed on Gin and his coming to accept his sexual orientation and working through his own feelings towards Hanai and getting them through. As it stands, Gin is pretty much happy-go-lucky but a flat character. We know little of his motivations and character other than loving Hanai. I’ll be continuing the series, even if it takes me a bit to dig into the next volume as it comes out slowly.

Title: Thornhedge
Author: T. Kingfisher
My Review:
What I loved most was the main character—quiet, gentle, and deeply layered. Rather than the typical hero who charges in with swords blazing, this story lingers in the gray areas of morality, asking what it means to protect others when your choices are limited. The conversations have a depth and heavy impact on our protagonists’ state of mind and eventually push her to some resolution. The prose is lyrical without being heavy, and the atmosphere builds a sense of unease while still carrying a thread of hope.

That said, while I thoroughly enjoyed it, I sometimes wished the story had been longer. The finale with the Goddess and the epilogue felt quite short. Certain parts felt like they ended just when I wanted more exploration, especially around the worldbuilding and side characters. Still, the restraint fits the fairytale tone—it’s sharp, concise, and intentional.

This was a great retelling of a classic fairytale. It was a short read so I recommend if you’re looking for something “sleeping beauty” but horror slow burn edition.

Title: Deep End
Author: Ali Hazelwood
My Review:
There were definitely parts of this book I enjoyed, but also plenty that didn’t work for me. Some characters were endearing and genuinely fun to read about, but unfortunately they only appeared briefly. The ones who had more page time often frustrated me in different ways.

Penelope, for example, was very easy to clock as superficial — not just in her relationships with others but also in how she viewed herself. Lukas felt like a copy-paste “green flag” character. While perfectly fine on paper, he didn’t stand out much until the end when we finally saw him fully commit to his new dream and goal. Scarlett, on the other hand, frustrated me with her tendency to run away from problems despite her need to always feel in control. On top of that, her sudden leaps in skill — doing better in German and effortlessly building neural networks from scratch — felt hollow and unearned. (When would a student athlete with premed learn about ml and NN ?? During their free time ? Cause last I checked it wasn’t a course typically offered to premed)

The climax showing up only in the last four or so chapters really irritated me. The buildup was smooth but dragged, and then everything important happened right at the end. The apology that followed did feel soothing, but I wish there had been more shown afterward to prove whether the words actually matched action when it came to our “villain.”

Overall, while there were glimpses of things I liked, the story often felt uneven or unfinished. I’ll take the resolution we got, but I can’t help but feel it could have been stronger or more impactful with deeper characters and more time breaking into the final resolution of the story.

Title: How to Solve Your Own Murder (Castle Knoll Files, #1)
Author: Kristen Perrin
My Review:
I especially enjoyed the journal entries of Frances. While I often disliked her as a person, her complexity made her far more likable by the end of the novel. She was deeply flawed—just like everyone else—but her self-awareness and honesty were oddly charming.

The characters were written so well that even the mere mention of certain names could evoke strong emotions. Emily, for example, infuriated me. I hated her, yet I couldn’t help but feel sorry for her. My sympathy didn’t excuse her actions, but I understood Frances’ perspective by the end of the story: no one deserves to have their story told for them, and no one deserves to have it cut short.

It was difficult to like anyone in this book. Every attempt to trust a character was met with hostility, deceit, or corruption, which was both frustrating and fascinating. The town being open to questions and to help Annie solve the murder felt believable, but I was shocked by just how deep the corruption ran. I’m surprised no one pulled the plug on it all.. but it is a book in which money holds a lot of weight.

The ending for me became clear as Frances started building relationships and pouring her energy into solving Emily’s disappearance. I wasn’t terribly surprised by the final twist, but I was stunned by Frances’ recklessness. The idea of a frail writer deliberately putting herself in danger—simply because she had a “plan”—felt both bold and unrealistic.. a bit longer and the story would have had an entirely different ending and meaning.

My biggest issue with the story was the pacing after the climax. The resolution felt rushed, moving too quickly through moments that deserved more emotional weight, particularly the family drama and reunion and long time fortunes finally ending. I had hoped for a slower, more reflective ending, maybe with Annie developing her own writing style inspired by Frances.

Overall, I’d give this book a 4/5. It delivered exactly what I expected from the synopsis: a gripping, character-driven mystery. I only wish the conclusion had taken more time to breathe.


A tiny footnote: it’s crazy how obsession bloomed into something so unhinged and unhealthy. And how history repeats itself in strange and unexpected ways

Title: Divine Rivals (Letters of Enchantment, #1)
Author: Rebecca   Ross
My Review:
I couldn't put this book down—I read it every chance I got. My thoughts are completely out of order but I’ll start expressing my feelings anyway I can.

The banter between Iris and Roman was absolute perfection. They really do have a way with words both in conversation and in the letters exchanged. The style of writing is honestly beautiful and easy to read. I could literally feel the tension between them electrically shifting from enemies to lovers. It was gratifying to see unfold throughout the story.

The rivals-to-lovers arc? A masterpiece. The atmosphere lingered in my mind all day. The stakes were perfectly set — forcing them to meet under harsh circumstances, only to be tested further as their choices grew more complicated and intertwined with the war. Watching them confront both themselves and each other was deeply satisfying.

It was a treat watching Iris fall for C-(no name spoilers!) without realizing it was Roman, all while actively hating him and wanting nothing to do with him. Their deep-rooted insecurities shaped them, but watching them slowly open up and help each other grow into better versions of themselves was beautiful.

I loved that the hardships they had experienced were brought up again and again in references to what thwarts them from moving on. Some authors seem to forget about how something traumatic might still affect someone even in mundane ways after it’s happened, but this one? PTSD HITS HARD. Guilt from a loved one’s passing and grenades all bring some sort of night terror or guilt riddled grief frequently for both characters. It made them more humane and real to me seeing how they slowly become more whole despite what happened in the past and continues happening.

I only wish they had been married longer... one single night, seriously?! But I get how it served as a way to set up the impending disaster that war brings💀

I am raging at Forest, Iris' brother-he single-handedly ruined my entire mood. I had so many expectations and how it played out was not it.
My heart shattered (my heart is still wrenching about it the next day) imagining how desperate Roman must have been to run after her on that injured leg for so long. I shed so many tears from dread, and that cliffhanger left me appalled.
I've never so desperately prayed to get the second book into my hands faster.

This may very well end up being my favorite book of the year. It's a stunning mix of fantasy, suspense, and beautifully crafted characters and worlds. The slow burn romance was intentional and exquisite-it had me yearning for a Roman
C. Kitt of my own.

Title: Fairest (The Lunar Chronicles, #3.5)
Author: Marissa Meyer
My Review:
I already knew Levana needed to have some sort of twisted past for her turning out how she did even till the very end. Levana's twisted cruel nature didn't happen overnight but through years and years of manipulation, pressure, and lack of self-love and understanding. I truly felt for her younger self as she really did have the best interest for Luna in her engagement in politics but her social reputation just diminished with the years. This doesn't really shed light on who Levana is now, but the book definitely goes out of its way to inform us that her karma was coming.

It's honestly a shame knowing that she was the better ruler for Luna but her mistrust and self-consciousness drove her to extreme measures when she could have had a much easier/happier life... I'm not sure "love" was the right word for what she felt for Evret, more like obsession and possession. Overall really unhealthy especially when she never trusted him with how she really looked even 10 years into marriage!

This book was quite exhausting because of all the small mistakes building up more and more that unfortunately could have been avoided if approached in a healthy way or like an intervention of some sort. Levana till the end had no one and was as alone from the start to the end...

It's safe to say her parents weren't a great influence considering that she needed to mention their blood on the bedroom floors were to make a nice color on her lips and that she had to pretend to grieve at their funeral. Channary was psychotic and how could one consider their torturer a good mentor and figure to model after... Evret honestly has so much warranted hate towards Levana that he really did not feel the need to guide Levana to the "right" path. All I've learned is that most of what was revealed to us is that anything can be justified whether right or wrong because it's subjective.

Again very good villain and stellar writing. It was jarring from start to end, keeping me wanting more.

Title: Cress (The Lunar Chronicles, #3)
Author: Marissa Meyer
My Review:
The best book thus far of the series! A huge part of it was due to Thorne and Cress. They are just so adorable together in their interactions. I'm looking forward to more of them in the next book I can barely wait to get started on it ("Winter" by Marissa Meyer).
Some huge Plot Twists I enjoyed:
-Thorne's background is hilarious in contrast to Cress's initial views/expectations of him. Though, I also do think Thorne's a good guy.
-I wish we had more time for Dr. Erland and Cress's father-daughter relationship to improve and get better. It was heartbreaking as these moments in books are always so frustrating. Saying you love someone doesn't come easy. Dr's last moments singing that lullaby for Cress was heartbreaking.
-The Dr figuring out that Letemosis was biological warfare that started from former Queen Chanary was surprising. Lunars were developing this for far longer than I thought...
-POOR SCARLET AND WOLF (TT_TT) They need each other and I feel heartbroken for Wolf and extremely worried for Scarlet.
-Princess Winter gives me weird vibes... Seeing the walls bleed yikes.. but I'm glad scarlet is getting medication.

Title: Scarlet (The Lunar Chronicles, #2)
Author: Marissa Meyer
My Review: I loved Scarlet and Wolf's story quite a lot. Wolf's innocent self and Scarlet's sharp tongue definitely added to the experience of their traveling together and bonding.  It was adorable though a bit rushed on the romance (this is a fairytale so haha as to be expected). They were so sappy but I love a bit of fluffy here and there. I started to look forward to their bit of the story more and more over Cinder's as it was getting irritating to see her so frustrated all the time over what she literally couldn't control. Her being Lunar and Cyborg was something she needed to accept in herself (<spoiler>at least by the end of the book but at least she makes a plan to move forward to find out more information about herself and practice becoming stronger for her people(lunars) as future Queen.</spoiler>) Hands down I can picture Thorne as Flynn Rider from Tangled. His sass and comments give me life from time to time and I think having him introduced and presented alongside Cinder really enhanced how fun of a character he is. Cinder and he will get along well and no wonder Kai is jealous of the two... They have some good chemistry (as friends together). Overall enjoyed this book a lot more than Cinder as it traveled at a faster pace and the side stories coming together at the end just really was satisfying.

Title: The Hate U Give (The Hate U Give, #1)
Author: Angie Thomas
My Review:
The Hate U Give - THUG
Just like how Tupac is still relevant this book remains relevant even to this current day even more so with the police brutality issues, the peaceful protests, and marches for black lives.

“What's the point of having a voice if you're gonna be silent in those moments you shouldn't be?”

One of the most captivating, heartwrenching books I've read that have brought me to tears from time to time. The tensions of confrontation and the silencing of outspoken words were breathtaking. It's also very frustrating as I know very well that the change Starr is looking towards in the future will one day come but slowly. We will always have people like Hailey being racist and we will always have the underlying problems of drugs and corrupt society. Still, there's also always someone willing to bring out their weapon, their voice, to speak out against those that try to silence them.
PS. I love Chris for all he is by treating her right and being so open to listen and understand. We need to be more like him in being willing to talk and understand rationally rather than be swayed by the opinions of others, pushing their own agenda onto others, and carelessly "joking" about matters that aren't jokes like Hailey.

Title: The Hazel Wood (The Hazel Wood, #1)
Author: Melissa Albert
My Review:
-DNF on Feb 1 2026- I can’t get into the book at all. I was starting to wonder if I’d ever like Alice or her life or even the others in her miserable life. It was starting to grate on me considerably and I literally just got through 50 pages.

Alice acts condescendingly towards everyone and only respects one person, her mother, Ella, whom she refers to with her first name despite her praises and worship of her. Ella isn’t a great person or even anyone shockingly exceptional, considering she didn’t even teach Alice basic life skills like “stranger danger”. Ella smokes and drinks and had her daughter making her martinis at the wave of her hand and had her addicted to smoking from a young age.

Alice lives her life on the road till her minor literary celebrity grandmother dies alone in her estate in the Hazel Wood. After her elusive grandmother’s death, her mother and she settle into New York, getting by working odd jobs. (The only thing I learned from Ella was to not hold serving trays higher than your waist because guys will take the chance to ogle your chest... in my opinion, that shit just sounds like the “you were asking for it” nonsense rather than teaching her how to call creeps out for their disgusting actions.)

Her mother bags a wealthy man 4 months into knowing him and gets Alice enrolled into a private school while Alice also works part-time at a pretentious cafe that turns into a bar in the evenings. Alice is both a very aggressive and an unagreeable person, making it hard not only for the other irritating people around her to like her but as a reader too. I couldn’t stand the literary snob vibes she’d give in addition to the anger issues (which she has no reason to dump on us like it’s world-building exposition).

The only part of the book I found remotely interesting and tolerable was the sparse tidbits of information on her grandmother Althea Proserpine’s life before she became a fairytale cult leader and hid herself away in her secluded estate in the woods. I got Alice’s obsession with wanting to know more about her family and her history, but that fizzled away faster than stale soda on a hot summer day.

Finch is a classmate at her private school; she used to think he was attractive until he opened his mouth, talking about her grandmother’s elusive book. After that revelation, she’d buried any affection she may have had into the dirt, which makes zero fucking sense to me. Like, girl, you want to read the damn book, right? Why don’t you ask him for his fucking copy? Or not whatever.

There’s nothing I like about Alice to the point I couldn’t care less about her or anyone else in the book. They all seem miserable and annoying to deal with. The only person whom I would be rooting for (Althea) already kicked the damn bucket. So I’m basically done. I don’t think I’ll be back to read this book anytime soon, not after how miserable it made me feel just 50 pages in.

"It's time to change the genre!"

Tall men with black hair-- just thank you Ruediger for existing in this (though you're a bit dense but sweet).

I have my suspicions SPOILER that Luca knows more than he's letting on especially with how he acts around others and how he instantly picked up mannerisms/learning whereas he struggled in the past. but it's like your usual Tragic Webtoon spinoff (turned comedy?)

The villainess here is not originally an integral part of the main story. She raises her sister's son until a member of the father's side of the family comes to pick the son up. In the original story, Luca (the son, heir to Winterwald) and Judith (the Villainess, Luca's Aunt) didn't have a great relationship. They would be pretty distant and bicker over everything and Judith would blame her lack of love/fortune in life on having to raise a child (Luca). With Luca's uncle (Ruediger) taking Luca away in the original leaving Judith with a handful of money as compensation was just the start of the tragedy as she becomes more and more greedy looking to make Luca into a cash cow essentially (eventually resulting in death).

I won't go into detail but after reincarnating into Judith's body the first thing she does is try and make amends with Luca before he leaves. However, he doesn't just leave, he brings Judith along this time as his "mother" (lol). The small changes that begin in the story soon snowball into a larger change in the genre... (to what I'm looking forward to is a Romantic Comedy).

Overall, it's a lovely first season and I can't wait to read season 2 when it's up!

It felt like secondhand embarrassment like when she said "Daddy" with such conviction at a work party where others could have been listening. It's just whiplash whenever it happens that I need a break and breather from the book. Lastly, several people are complaining about the italics, but in audio, it's not an issue truly so I'll give that a pass.

Now to review the characters. I liked Jack a lot. He was sensible and all his actions made sense from start to finish. Elsie was harder to follow and relate to... even when I'm also a woman in STEM (computer engineering and electrical engineering). So it was pleasant to dig into Jack's background and mentality through his every move.

The twist was great! I liked the betrayal, it just took forever to get to that point. Sure there were signs, but nothing truly off-putting to start warning and alerting readers of the red flags. It was a slow burn. I liked the final conclusion, but it left a lot to be answered like Elsie's family situation.

Title: The Very Secret Society of Irregular Witches
Author: Sangu Mandanna
My Review:
I have to admit I was having a hard time getting into the book for a while because of the internal conflicts Mika Moon was having within herself and society (as a whole). She felt her passions and identity of a witch had to be buried deep within and could not share it with others other than with a facade of an internet witchy influencer.

It was only really when she talked about her upbringing that I started to understand and empathize with her situation and feelings. Having no real roots and lack of connection with anyone in her life other than Primrose (who kept things from her and actively encouraged distancing themselves from one another) that Mika felt she had no home in the vast world.

I adored every character who brought part of themselves into this tiny world built in Nowhere House. I loved the communication of the characters! Miscommunication is the bane of my existence but this book tackled it head first and it was gratifying to see someone I’d grown to understand and admire take a stand for others when they’ve been raised to be mistrustful and weary of everyone.

This book felt like a warm cup of tea on a rainy day with the fire crackling.

Title: The Specimen
Author: Jaima Fixsen
My Review:
Wow ok so I started reading this little by little every so often I went out for a drive picking my sibling up. It was a really really slow burn suspenseful experience. I enjoyed the story and the diverse characters and how the story developed slowly with every page. It had many moments that hit hard emotionally in a tearful way and one that made me want to drive a pitchfork through the antagonist. I had hoped for a side story developing the found family theme but overall I’m content with how the story unfolded and had wrapped up. It was a great read following the true crime story of the infamous Burke and Hare murders whose killings supplied an anatomy school’s operations and research.

Made me grateful for the more strict medical/ human rights laws we have in place in modern day to prevent and protect us from tragedies as in the book.

I recommend it to those looking to sink their teeth into something unsettling and touching. I retold the book to my family at most sittings when they had asked for a follow up to the tale and it was fun to watch and hear about their reactions to certain parts of the story as it unfolded for us.

Title: What Moves the Dead (Sworn Soldier, #1)
Author: T. Kingfisher
My Review:
What Moves the Dead is a gothic horror retelling of Edgar Allan Poe’s “The Fall of the House of Usher,” this novella stands firmly on its own with eerie brilliance and a fresh, modern voice. It was unsettling, immersive, and laced with slow creeping dread. The pacing is almost perfect, with tension that builds steadily through eerie details and clever foreshadowing.

The protagonist, a sharp-witted female soldier, brings a refreshing perspective. Her subtle commentary and occasional, well-placed personal insights give the story emotional weight while also emphasizing the horror of her surroundings. Her character challenges social conventions without the narrative ever feeling preachy especially with the interactions between Ms. Potter and Easton.

While the dry sarcasm adds some levity, it sometimes feels overdone. The ending, too, feels a little too neat—lacking the urgency or chaos that the story seemed to be heading toward. I had hoped the antagonist had put up more of a fight rather than to simply claim “a peace existence (though they had claimed the life of someone already and had wrecked the local ecosystem).

Still, this is a chilling, memorable read with atmosphere to spare. But man reanimated corpses definitely weren’t on my 2025 bingo card 😅.

My Review:
Vol. 3
Episode 25 ~ 34

Gods this was the most heartbreaking volume I’ve ever read on webtoons. My soul felt wrecked by the sheer amount of pain Rieta experienced from her PTSD reliving the nightmare that was loss from a pandemic. Killian has so much depth to his character.. his actions in choosing to slap her to her senses was so devastating to see. You can tell his first choice of actions in the situation (as with others I’m sure) has always been brute force and being gentle as an afterthought. I applaud the author for their ability to convey this level of sentiment and understanding of trauma and grief riddled guilt into this volume. I love how Killian is also displayed in more way now. We all know of his intelligence and wits in leadership and taking charge against his step mother. But now we see how his past’s deeds are helping him out now in current day.
